utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody around the court today. Before we call the case, just a small housekeeping matter. I won't go into details because the witness is here already. The Chamber received an urgent motion for protective measures yesterday, and because of its urgency, what we want to find out is whether the parties, or particularly the Defence, would be in a position to give maybe an oral response not now but at the beginning of the next break, and then maybe we can see how to proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can certainly do that. We were anticipating lodging a response this afternoon, but certainly we can give the indication after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's much appreciated. Sorry, Mr. Robson, do I understand you to say you would be in a position to give some oral comments at the beginning of the next break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate it. Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have appearances for today. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio, assisted today by our intern, Emma Berry, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, colleagues from the Prosecution, everybody in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson representing the Defence of General Delic, with assistants Lejla Gluhic and Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Divjak, may I remind you that at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, you made a declaration to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just remind you that you are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth even today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, General Divjak. Yesterday, at the end of the court --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. We were discussing the Mujahedin, and you told the Chamber about the first time that you had heard about their presence, and you testified about a meeting on the 18th of June, 1993. Do you recall your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting of 18 June 1993, when was the next time that you heard about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not official, it was not any official meeting. It was during some talks in 1994 and 1995 between me, myself, and the people who were in the Staff, people who at the time were at the forward command post in Zenica or Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And we will get to that meeting, because it has a videotape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But first I'd like the witness to be shown Exhibit 271, please. Sir, I'd like you to read this document, since it is short.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Thank you, sir. You don't need to read it into the record, just read it. Have you had a chance to read it, look at it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you showed me this paper the day before yesterday, which was the first time I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And this paper is eight days after the 18th -- excuse me, it is a month and eight days after the meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this is at document authorising Sakib Mahmuljin to carry out negotiations on behalf of General Delic with regard to the Mujahedin; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you were never aware of this action that was being taken?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of the existence of this authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I can put away this document, and I would like the witness to be shown --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- document P01461.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You also showed me this document two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is that the first time that you had seen this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this document is dated the 12th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, the 12th of August, 1993, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And it is -- this is also, I should correct for the record, marked as Exhibit 272.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this is an order or a proposal, I should say, from Commander Hadzihasanovic with regard to incorporating the El Mujahedin -- naming the El Mujahedin Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, the way it is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you were never aware of this proposal, this action that was being proposed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of either this proposal or the action proposed in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we put away this document, and I'd like the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you -- what I have marked as P01466 which has been marked already as Exhibit 273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that you call it by the exhibit number that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And forget about the "P0".

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, when is the first time that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the proofing session at your office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And would you agree that this is a document dated the 13th of August, which is a day after the previous document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it bears the date 13th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And it's signed -- it's an order signed by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it be scrolled up a bit, because I cannot see the signature. Yes, Commander Delic's signature is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then I'd like the witness to be shown -- highlight the first page, Roman numeral II, "Mobilisation Preparations."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, this says: "The order is to replenish the El Mujahedin Detachment with foreign volunteers currently on the territory of the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility. These people keep the weapons and other equipment which they already had been issued to them." Is that what that says?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the order of the army commander says under item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So as deputy commander to General Delic and to the army, were you aware of any of these actions that were taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the previous two documents which you showed to me, and the one that you are showing to me right now, I don't know anything about those.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at some point was there a change in the position of the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, Hadzihasanovic was the commander. Later, General Sakib Mahmuljin was appointed in his stead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you ever attend any meetings with General Delic and Sakib Mahmuljin together?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one of the meetings were not only the two of them but also the corps commanders. That was a regular briefing on combat readiness. It took place in Zenica, and I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how often were these regular meetings being held?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have meetings in the Staff, at the Staff, in Sarajevo every morning, at the forward command post probably every morning, and once or twice every two months the commander organised meetings with corps commanders. As far as I can recall, I cannot remember the exact date, but as far as I can recall, I attended one of those meetings. And I can remember something which may be interesting; that is, that it was General Delic's birthday on that day or around that time, so that I congratulated him on his birthday on behalf of the Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But if you only attended one of those meetings, how are you aware that there were other meetings between General Delic and Sakib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll stand corrected if I'm wrong, but I don't think it's been established that there were meetings between General Delic and Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I was going to show Your Honours where we discussed it. Line 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 14, page 6, the question was -- where was it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's off the screen now. That's why I was trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At line 14: "And did you ever attend any meetings with General Delic and Sakib Mahmuljin together?" And the answer was: "At one of the meetings, there were not only the two of them but also the corps commanders ..." And the discussion is developed along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but my understanding from the evidence is at no stage has General Divjak stated that there were other meetings between General Delic and Sakib Mahmuljin, which was obviously put to the witness in the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It does say, "at one of the meetings," but I will rephrase the question, Your Honour, and ask the witness straight out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any other meetings that took place between General Delic and Sakib Mahmuljin, other than the one that you attended with them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for individual meetings between General Delic and General Mahmuljin, I'm not aware of any meetings between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Are you aware of regular corps meetings where the two of them would be in attendance along with other corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that meetings were being held outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know who attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at those meetings. I don't know who attended them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of any reports that were submitted by General Mahmuljin to General Delic regarding the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information. I don't know that General Mahmuljin ever informed General Delic about the operations of the Mujahedin or the use or the combat operations carried out by Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like the witness, please, to be shown Exhibit P01783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, exhibit or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, it's a pre-trial exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you have an opportunity to review this document on Sunday or before Sunday?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge, you showed me this document, and we commented on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what -- what were your comments with regard to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I raise an objection at this stage. The witness has clearly stated that he was not aware of any reports being sent by General Mahmuljin to General Delic, and this is such a document, so this is a document the witness has never seen before prior to the briefing session and I would submit that to get the General to comment upon it at this stage would be inviting speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would like to ask him about the contents of the document, not about whether he saw it -- I would like to ask him about his knowledge of certain matters that are contained within the document. And as deputy commander of the army, he was in a high-enough position that I think he should be asked about the matters that are contained in this document. Whether it gets admitted or not through this witness is another matter, but I should be allowed to ask him questions about what's contained in the document, the topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you need the document to ask him about the content?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, it just -- it will facilitate me having to read -- not me having to read items into the record, but I can -- I can certainly -- I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are not intending to tender the document into evidence through this witness; you just want to ask him about the contents? Is that what I understand you to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. I think we may tender it, but it also may be helpful to know -- mark it for identification so that later on if another witness speaks about this document, we know that this is the same document that the General was shown and was asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed for those limited purposes. But just before you do, just by looking at the two documents that are appearing on the screen, are we clear that the one is a translation of the other? The one seems to be very sparsely written on, and the other one is very richly written on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I don't read B/C/S, so it's hard for me to say for sure, but the spacing is different. The English version is double-spaced, versus the single space, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want confirmation that it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, it appears to me the numbers are the same, the date. If I can look at the numbers at the top of the B/C/S document. 21 of 01/11. 1849/94. It appears to be the same document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the date of this document is the 10th of October, 1994; would you agree with that? Or, well, sorry, excuse me. Sir, it says in the -- I'll withdraw that question and start over so there's no objection. Are you aware that there were problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just I don't think the record caught what Judge Harhoff said. Could it reflect that the document is dated the 10th of August, 1994, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You just wanted to mention that, to correct that October mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have that, please? Can the record show that the date of the document is the 10th of August, 1994, and not the 10th of October, 1994. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, as deputy commander of the army, were you aware --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, as deputy commander of the army, were you aware that there was an established El Mujahedin Detachment by 1994 which was an independent unit comprised of two companies and a command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this harks back to the witness's earlier answer when he explained that he didn't hear anything else, apart from an informal discussion, between members of the Main Staff and himself at some stage between 1994 and 1995, so -- my colleague also -- we also object on the basis that it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, if the witness can answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just respond to the objection, Madam. Forget about the witness for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, as deputy commander of the army, were you aware that there were concerns expressed by corps commanders with regard to problems with foreigners who came in to the army and tried to change customs and norms and behaviour of the local population?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, could you be more specific? What corps commanders are you talking about, because the corps commanders did not have any problems with this unit, if you are referring to the El Mujahid unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how do you know that corps commanders didn't have any problems with this unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th and 7th Corps, there were no such units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you were aware that there was a unit in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already established that we knew that, when that unit was about to be comprised within the 3rd Corps. In the reports -- we had reports in early 1994 about the existence of that unit, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So when I asked you earlier about your knowledge of the unit, you did know something about the unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat. I said that it was the first time that I learned about it, on the 18th of June, as did the rest of the people in the Staff, when we asked that those groups of foreigners should be returned to where they had come from or that a unit be set up of them within the framework of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later, I learned about the existence of that unit. I learned about that in 1994. I learned about some of the -- their activities. No, I learned about the existence of the unit, but not about the activities that you presented to me right now. So I didn't learn about them from our meetings. I just heard that they had participated together with some of the brigades of the 3rd Corps in defending parts of the territory in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you said you learned about that in 1994, learned about some of their activities. What activities did you learn about, and how did you learn about these activities?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry, that's the interpretation coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We haven't -- we missed completely what the witness just said. I could ask the question again, if that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My question was: Now, you said you learned about that in 1994, learned about some of their activities. What activities did you learn about, and how did you learn about these activities?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in 1994, there were two parts of the Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a smaller group that I headed in the Staff in Sarajevo, and a larger group that was in Kakanj. We regularly received reports, albeit in a summary form, from the various corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In one of the reports from the 3rd Corps, there was a mention of the El Mujahid Detachment which, together with other brigades of the 3rd Corps, took part in the fighting or better to say the defence of the territory of the 3rd Corps against the aggressor. I cannot recall exactly which units it cooperated with, but that was the information we had. And as for the documents you're showing me, perhaps we can analyse a couple of sentences from it, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sure, yes, that would be fine, sir, if you want to draw the Court's attention to certain aspects and tell them what you want to say about that, that would be appropriate. You have to first direct us to the paragraph, if you would, so that everyone knows what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second part on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Which paragraph, if you could count them, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It begins with the 12th paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I have them marked on my copy, Your Honours, so I can go to it pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You're talking about line 12?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It begins with: "One of such units ..." Or, rather: "One such unit which exists in the municipalities of Zenica and Travnik is the ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. That is the second paragraph, Your Honours, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire passage was something that I learned for the first time during the proofing sessions. Before that, I had no knowledge of any of the content in this paragraph. In the reports we received from the 3rd Corps, there was only mention of a unit. There was never mention of any command or establishment, and just recently you told me that there were two companies. I never knew about that before I saw this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Are there other -- are there other comments you would like to make about other sections of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said at the beginning, I want to reiterate that this was a joint report. However, it was drafted by the Minister of the Interior of Zenica. It was signed by the 3rd Corps commander as well, though, since he agreed with the report. This report forwards information to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the Minister of the Interior. Therefore, this document was not sent only -- could we please go back to the top? In addition to being sent to the Staff of the Supreme Command, it was also sent to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have ten minutes to go, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like the witness to be shown a videotape. Can we mark this for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 350, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Videotape P06017. And there is a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like to stop the tape. Okay. Well, actually, after the next -- at the end of this speaker, I'd like to stop the tape, please. It's one more line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, you can stop the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you identify persons who are in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the other things you put to me earlier, I conclude from the transcript that this was a mixed delegation. On one side, there was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the other the HVO unit commands. I can see that the delegations were headed by civilian commanders, or rather to the right-hand side we see Mr. Ganic, who at the time was president of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the left-hand side, the person who spoke towards the end of the footage is Mr. Zubak who at the time was vice-president of the Federation. Just to remind you, in case you don't know, after the conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, with the support of the Croatian Army, the Geneva Peace Accord was signed and the Federation founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I just want you to identify other persons at this meeting, if you could.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you about the people on the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina side that I can recognise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please do that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second person with a cap on his head is General Bilajac. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remember that the first person is Hindic Kemal, the one with the moustache. The second person is Bilajac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Madam Sartorio, who is the first -- how does the record know who the first person is and the second person is and who Ganic is, the president of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness to be more specific, Your Honours, but it looks like it's now time for a break, although I'm willing to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't we take our break at quarter past 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but my understanding was yesterday I was told I had 2.17 as of yesterday, but if I may -- okay. All right, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify persons on the side of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person closest to us with the moustache --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: On the right --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is Kemal Hindic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the screen in front of you, the person with the moustache who is closest to us.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his name is Kemal Hindic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know the person next to him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Rifat Bilajac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you identify anyone -- the person beside him? Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person leaning against his arm is Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That looks to be the fourth person in from the screen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The third person; okay. And can you identify the fourth person?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next is General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. There is a person with -- the person with the hat you've identified is --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rifat Bilajac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Then there appears to be a person next to him with what I see is a person with --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic, president of the Federation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this the person whose face we cannot see, we just see the hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can only see his hair, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you are able to identify him as Mr. Ganic, without seeing his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just asking, I'm just asking. Are you able to identify him without seeing his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know what his hair looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is that the same person who you referred to as resting on his arm or does that arm belong to the person to his right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It belongs to the person on the right side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't belong to Ganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to Ganic, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see General Delic also at the table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence position -- well, the Defence position is that this is -- it's a difficult situation for the witness to go through the list and identify witnesses. We would have no objection if the Prosecution were -- if it were able to produce a suitable extract or printout from the page, and then to show it to the witness at some stage during the course of today, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. May I suggest something? Your Honour, may I suggest something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll give you a chance in a second, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what we could do is freeze the screen and ask the witness to mark on it. No, we can't do that. A hard copy, we'll make a hard copy and ask the witness to mark on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just find out what the witness had to say. Did you want to say something, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we should go on with the footage, because we will see those people much better later on when they address the rest of the people around the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would just -- Your Honour, I just want the witness, if he can, to identify the next speaker whose initials are RD, and then I would like to proceed with the tape. And then we can go back to identification, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does he identify RD?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask him if he knows who is speaking. But I'd like the Court to know, before you -- who the person is before we get into the whole discussion. So if we could just play a few minutes of RD, ask the witness if he knows who's speaking. Then we can listen to the whole thing. That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're now abandoning your attempt to identify the people around the table?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think we can go back to that, time permitting, but the Prosecution would like to get in the content of the next part of this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you please, ma'am. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we start the tape?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can we stop the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the voice of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's the end of this portion. Your Honour, I would ask that this videotape be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The videotape is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit number 351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Forgive me for just asking for a piece of clarification, Mrs. Sartorio. Where was this location and when was the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And which meeting was it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where -- when it took place, I don't know where it took place, but judging by the composition of the delegations, I can say that the two delegations are one on the part of the Army of B and H and the other on the part of the HVO, or rather the other component of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO delegation is headed by Mr. Zubak, who at the time was vice-president of the Federation of B and H. The Army of B and H delegation is headed by Mr. Ejup Ganic who at the time was president of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know -- would you have an idea as to what year this might be?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can only be 1994, after the Washington Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that's as far as we can go in terms of the date and the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We ask the document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking about this video clip?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I was under the impression -- never mind. If I may ask a few more questions, Your Honours, if you would indulge me, to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of meetings between General Delic and President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Are you aware of any -- how often they communicated?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you recall meeting with myself and other persons from the OTP on Sunday and Monday?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you recall that we discussed a lot of issues, including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're dealing with examination-in-chief, and it would appear that prosecuting counsel is attempting to cross-examine her own witness, so I raise an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to ask the witness if he can recall and reiterate the discussion that we had on certain topics. It's not -- I'm not trying to impeach the witness. Under Rule 90(F), the Trial Chamber has the discretion to exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence if it leads to -- if it's effective for the ascertainment of the truth, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, please ask me specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. The madam was talking to me, sir, at this point. She was not asking you a question. Just hold on. Are you done, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, when I asked you about communications between General Delic and Mr. Izetbegovic, do you recall what you told me?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put a specific question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That is my specific question. I'm asking if you recall the answer that you gave to me when I asked you how -- if you knew how often General Delic and President Izetbegovic communicated on a regular basis -- or communicated, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I said that it was probably daily, whether directly or over various means of communication, since the army commander was duty-bound to brief on the army's activities. I did not mention the frequency, though, and I spoke about the things that were supposed to take place. To continue, General Delic, as a member of the War Presidency, as well as me occasionally, participated at the sessions. Based on the two session documents that you put to me, you probably know that there were over 200 different sessions in the two or three years of the war. Should I go on? We were witnesses to the fact that General Delic, when President Izetbegovic would visit the units, escorted him. It was his duty. And when we discussed this, I never meant their private contacts, or rather I meant their ex officio duties in particular, the army commander's duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you say, "I never meant their private contacts," what do you know about their private contacts?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, I asked you yesterday the following question, and it's at page 31, lines 15 to 16, on LiveNote. Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't mean to interrupt you, if you were going to -- okay. I asked you yesterday: "Sir, did you ever receive reports in 1994 and 1995 with regard to discipline problems in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?" Do you recall my question to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall your question, but by your leave can I expand on that? We did not receive information only in regards the 7th Muslim Brigade, but also in respect of all units that would at certain points in time actually breach their responsibility or did not honour military responsibility -- military discipline in their respective zones of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My specific question to you, however, was whether or not you received reports about the 7th Muslim Brigade. I'm not asking you about reports of other units. Your answer was: "In any case, those of us in Sarajevo --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the prosecuting counsel is now putting the answer of the witness given during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, it's during yesterday's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise. I withdraw that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your response at page 31, lines 20 through 22, was: "In any case, those of us in Sarajevo did not receive any specific information on anything negative that would have to do with any activities of the 7th Muslim Brigade." Do you recall that being your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to my recollection, allow me to continue, I also said that when I stayed in Zenica for the first time in September 1993, that at that time we received information -- actually, people directly told me that they were fearful of the conduct -- certain forms of conduct of members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and I adduced the example of the way in which they went about their morning workouts, morning exercises, fitness exercises, in the part of town where Bosniaks lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, my specific --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's correction, "where non-Bosniaks also lived."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But my specific question to you is whether you received reports, and yesterday you stated, as I just said, you didn't receive any specific information. So did you or did you not receive specific information upon which you could base your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the reports which we received from the 3rd Corps, there was no specific information about the conduct of the 7th Brigade. I repeat that I learned about this when, in September, I was in Zenica. And if my memory serves me well, I also referred to the fact that the International Committee of the Red Cross also exhibited interest in ascertaining the actual state of affairs in the so-called "prison" in the music school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, sir, giving a statement to an OTP investigator in September of 2005?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what segment you mean. What I stated in September 2005?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The first question I'm asking is if you recall being interviewed by an OTP investigator which was audio-recorded.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which one you mean. I certainly do recall it. I don't know what part you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just I'm asking -- I'm not asking about a specific part of the statement. I'm asking you whether you remember giving a statement in 2005, September.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you arrived in The Hague on Saturday, did you -- you were given some materials to review, and part of these materials was this statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And during the proofing session, do you recall whether or not you made any changes to your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not make any changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you recall in the interview and do you recall from reading your transcript that you were asked questions about the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but can you please repeat what those questions were for my benefit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, do you recall what you said to the investigator with regard to the 7th Muslim Brigade being responsible, to a certain extent, for atrocities over non-Bosniak people? Do you recall saying that to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know I've already objected once along these lines, but if prosecuting counsel is going to put a number of these types of questions to the witness, I question whether, in reality, she's really trying to impeach her own witness. So again I object on the basis that the Prosecutor is trying to lead the witness to the desired response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to refresh his recollection to see if he recalls certain prior topics that were discussed and what he discussed. I only have two more of these types of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only problem, Madam Sartorio, is that it seems as if you're just not -- your witness is not cooperating with you, and the whole situation does appear to be like you are now trying to impeach the witness because he's refusing to give you the answers you probably are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking to put the case before the Chamber. I'm not looking for specific answers, Your Honour. But I think the Chamber should be apprised of all aspects of what this witness has said about certain topics he talked about in court today so that Your Honours can assess what to believe and what not to believe with regard to all the witnesses. And it's not -- I'm not trying to designate this witness as a hostile witness. I know that there are other cases in the Tribunal, particularly the Milosevic case, where this was allowed to be done without declaring the witness a hostile witness. And if he remembers, he remembers. If he doesn't, then -- then he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have in front of us his statement, so why don't you just bring your witness directly to the place in the statement where you want to go, and let's take it from there. Let's keep it simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But, however, I think -- I don't know if you have the whole statement. Do you have the transcripts of the statement? It's several transcripts. It's several hundred pages long. But I do have the page number and reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What we have is the witness statement dated 23rd September 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right, but if you look at the last part of the statement, it says that we will continue on to a tape-recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't you just put the tape-recording or whatever the page is of the statement that you want to refer the witness to. Let the witness see and identify it as his statement, if it is his statement, and verify it through his signature, if the signature is there, and refer him to the specific part of the statement that you want him to talk about. For purposes of the objection, we will allow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall giving a tape-recorded statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I gave a statement. I don't know right now what statement specifically you're talking about. And I am really embarrassed to hear His Honour say that we are not cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, His Honour -- never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll show the witness three pages from T000-2915, side A and B of a tape-recorded statement, and ask if he recalls this interview. Could we put that on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are not going to raise an objection right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not going to raise an objection, that's fine. Sit down, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting no interpretation. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we sort out the interpretation, first, Madam Vidovic? I'm hearing no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Your Honour? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear that voice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I cannot hear counsel now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps I -- well, anyway, created this confusion. Your Honours, if the Prosecutor could, in future, give us in advance, for instance, we could have been given these parts of the statement this morning, we would be grateful. I'm not going to raise an objection right now to the use of this part of the statement, but we should like to be able to prepare ourselves beforehand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honour, in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. You do concede you haven't given the Defence this part of the statement that you are now going to use?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I didn't -- they have it, Your Honour, they have it, and they've been given the statement in disclosure. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why, then, do you say it's okay in the future?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, because of out of courtesy I WOULD let them know this morning I was going to be going to this particular page, that's all. I would try to be as cooperative as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have to tell them about the page you want to go to when you have disclosed the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour. I'm just saying out of courtesy in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read this, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is being read?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could you keep scrolling down, please? The next page, actually, top of the next page. Top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, we're five minutes beyond break time. Shouldn't the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I just have this last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall saying that the 7th Muslim Brigade is responsible, to a certain extent, for atrocities over non-Bosniak people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: On the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is DB?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It is the interpreter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we going to get an answer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here -- it is written here that I stated that the 7th Muslim Brigade is partly responsible for what was happening in Zenica and around Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is that -- is that your belief, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm struggling to grasp the relevance of these questions, because as far as the Defence are aware, General Delic is not indicted for any acts caused or carried out by the 7th Muslim Brigade. So I just wonder where the questions are leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour, and ask another one, if I may, to make it easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said you were asking the last question before we go to break. Can we go to break or is it not convenient?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, at page 33, lines 23 to 26, you said: "It states here, it is written here, that I stated that the 7th Muslim Brigade is partly responsible for what was happening in Zenica and around Zenica." And you can see, from the transcript, the English says, "The 7th Muslim Brigade is responsible to a certain extent for atrocities over non-Bosniak people." My first question to you is: What is it that you said to the OTP investigator? Which was it? Is this an incorrect translation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is written here, which is that the 7th Muslim Brigade also bears responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Is that your -- sorry. Is that the end of your sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I explain the idea? I've just confirmed what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before you explain, sir: Was that the end of your sentence, that what is written here, according to you, is that the Muslim Brigade also bears responsibility, full stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the end here in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may I continue? If we are speaking about the war period, what I knew is what I said, about what I knew in 1993 when I was in Zenica. When I say that the 7th Muslim Brigade bears certain responsibility for incorrect conduct towards non-Bosniak people, that refers to the information I gained after the war and what I read in the mass media. Reverting to the period that we are talking about, I did not know that the brigade was doing anything that was in contravention of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. We do have a still photograph of the meeting, if the witness could indicate on the photograph the names of the persons he can identify as present, and then we'll ask that that be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in response to an earlier question by Judge Harhoff, the Prosecution can offer information as to the source of the videotape and the date of that videotape, if the Court would like that. The date was 13 November of 1994, and it was received from the ARBiH Archives, Reference number 6 -- G, sorry, GSH3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the videotape that shows the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection. It was the Prosecutor testifying, what the date of the footage was. They should bring a witness from the Archives to testify on that. I am simply objecting in the same way they objected to my questions yesterday, when they said I was testifying. It is not up to the Prosecutor to introduce any information on the source or the date. We will not accept any such information as relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going to bring in an archivist who will confirm that date. I just wanted to bring it to the Court's attention to put it into context, since we can't call the archive person until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So should we then mark the photograph for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Not the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The videotape itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, the remark can be disregarded by the Court, about the date of the videotape, if it so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Objection upheld. Madam Sartorio - sorry, just before you stand up - you have asked that a photograph be placed on the ELMO, ma'am. Are you sitting down or are you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, I was talking to my senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. It's just that your opposite number was standing already and I wanted to be sure that you are finished before I allow him to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I am finished, Your Honour, as soon as the witness can write on the photograph the persons he can identify. That's what -- that's what we're waiting for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first person on the photograph is Kemal Hindic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please write that on the photograph right there, just write it, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we give the witness a pen, please, that can write?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Divjak, do you think you can print so that we are able to read, rather than cursive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, but may I write it in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean you are able to -- you can't print in Latin? Okay. Do what is best for you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] These are the people I can recognise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is Mr. Ganic in the photo? I thought you indicated he was in the photo in your testimony. Did you mark that? If you know.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His Honour asked whether I can recognise him only by his hair. Therefore, I'm not sure. But I did see the entire footage, and I know that Ganic addressed everyone at the meeting. That is why I said that between Mr. Bilajac and Mr. Delic, it is Mr. Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness -- you have the testimony and the photograph. I would like him to put who he thinks is Mr. Ganic on the photograph. If you would, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. We move that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- that this be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The photograph is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the photo now. Thank you very much, Madam Sartorio. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Divjak. My name is Nicholas Robson, and together with my colleagues, we represent General Rasim Delic. I'd like to start my cross-examination just briefly dealing with the situation in Sarajevo at the start of the war. Now, as deputy commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were primarily based in Sarajevo during the war, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that from May 1992, Sarajevo was placed under a siege by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially as of mid-April 1992, and completely as of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from the date of the complete siege, if I can call it that, the siege lasted until the end of the war; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We believe it lasted for 1.260 days or 44 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: From May 1992, the time of the complete blockade, it's correct, isn't it, that the sending of information and orders from the Main Staff to other parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became very difficult?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, we know that you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecution in September 2005. Do you recall discussing with those persons some of the communication problems that were experienced by the Main Staff in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo itself and outside of Sarajevo with the subordinate units which, for example, were under a siege such as the ones in Srebrenica, Gorazde, it was very difficult to communicate with Mostar as well, for the simple reason that the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have modern communication equipment. We often used the simple field telephone connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can pause you there, General, you mentioned that you didn't have modern communication equipment. It's right that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to rely upon radio amateurs to send information and to communicate with some of the places you mentioned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Also, is it true to say that communication to the Main Staff in Sarajevo could also be disrupted by the weather conditions in place at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to poor weather conditions and also because there was interference, technical interference, on the part of the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is this radio communication that we're talking about that could be affected by weather and interference by the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do with all means of communications, but first and foremost radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And as a result of these difficulties, it's true, isn't it, that a report could start to be received at the Main Staff and then suddenly it would stop because of disruption?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases in particular when radio amateurs were involved, when they conveyed messages from Srebrenica or Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the point that I was trying to make was that on occasions at the Main Staff, a situation could arise whereby a report would start to be received and then suddenly it would halt before the whole report being transmitted or being received at the Main Staff; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that detail. I was not in a position to know. It is a technical matter, and those who were in charge of that can tell you better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. General, you have testified previously in 1997 during the Zejnil Delalic case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could refer you to testimony that you gave during that case on the 28th of October, 1997. And the reference is page 8.437, line 21. You said that one of the first targets of the aggression was the telecommunication system. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I also believe I stated then, and I can confirm it now, that out of ten radio relay devices that used to be controlled by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, first the JNA and then the VRS occupied those positions, thus effectively cutting off the government's connections to the rest of the country and abroad. What we were left with, in terms of the government, were only three radio relay hubs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: During the Delalic case, you went on to say, at line 23: "It was not possible to use the electronics communication to pass information in a timely fashion to the subordinate staffs. It happened that certain information or orders would take several days to get through via messengers." Is that right, what you said during the trial in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly to mean by that that messengers were used to deliver reports from and to the Main Staff headquarters by hand?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I stated this, what I had in mind is exactly what you put now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And for those messengers to get to and from the Main Staff headquarters in Sarajevo, is it correct that they would have to cross the Sarajevo airfield, which was an extremely dangerous place, particularly until the tunnel was built?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, General, would you agree with me that during the war, it was a real problem for the Main Staff headquarters to obtain information from subordinate units in the field about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right when you say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct that these difficulties with communication had a detrimental impact on the ability to command and control Bosnian Army units in the field?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. One of the aggravating factors that had to be counted on by the army was the lack of up-to-date means of communication. Therefore, it often happened that orders and reports would be delayed or late and would arrive on occasion even after the time they envisaged for something to be done had already lapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And on that point, yesterday in your testimony you described how information came in to the Main Staff every day. Bearing in mind the conditions that you've just described, is it fair to say that it was extremely difficult for the Main Staff to receive clear and accurate information from subordinate units in the field each day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned the reports, it only had to do with corps reports. The Staff was in no position to receive information from its subordinate units, from brigades or detachments, for example. But even that could not be fully relied upon in terms of time and when something was being dispatched. Some activity may have already taken place without the Staff knowing or being able to react to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you said, "but even that could not be fully relied upon," are you talking there about the corps reports?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the reports coming from the corps. In view of its limited technical ability, the corps reports would boil down to the most relevant and important information only. They would not provide any further details about such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that the problems with communication was one of the main reasons for the Bosnian Army to establish a forward command post in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem you mentioned, that is something that we at the Staff were aware of as early as 1992. It was our position that the Staff would have to be moved to Igman as early as September. However, it was not done until a certain time towards the end of 1993. With a view to handle the defence more efficiently, it was told that the Staff should move outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I'll come to the places where the Staff moved to in a moment, but before I do so, if I could deal with another matter. Yesterday, you were asked by the Prosecution the date by which the organisational structure of the ARBiH was functioning and operating. Do you remember being asked that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not, but I wasn't asked about whether it was functional and operational. I said that the TO was established on the 9th. In June, it was renamed to become the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And until June 1993, it carried out combat tasks all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was organised at that time as well. As to whether it was functional, that is debatable, perhaps not in this courtroom but among experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, General, where you say the TO was established on the 9th, that was the 9th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th of April, 1992. It was when the TO Staff was formed, and it was then that the TO Staff established communication with municipal TO staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also said, I believe, that it managed to establish communication with 76 or 77 municipal TOs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, concerning the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you've mentioned, "As to whether it was functional, that is debatable." Is it correct to say that it took a considerable period of time for the Bosnian Army to establish itself and to create all the different units at various levels?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are talking about organising, it was organised until the end of 1992. It was comprised of independent detachments, units and brigades. Five corps were formed as well. However, the basic problem were the lack of materiel and equipment needed for those units to be able to carry out their tasks. However, during that one year, irrespective of the fact whether it was functional or not, it was sufficient to stop the aggressor's attacks and intentions they had, and they were stopped at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: General, just returning back to the formation of the units of the Bosnian Army, is it correct that you, yourself, were involved in the formation of brigades during November 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please explain. Why are you referring to November 1992, in particular? I believe the brigades were formed in June and July 1992, not in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, General, if I could refer you to your testimony during the Delalic case which you gave on the 28th of October, 1997. And the reference is page 8.461, line 21. You were asked about the formation of the brigades, and your response was: "But the brigades were in the process of being formed, because one of my main tasks which I received on the 2nd of November, 1992, from the Supreme Command was to assist in forming brigades in Neretvica and Jablanica." Is it right that you were --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of the brigades, but those particular brigades in that particular area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is correct. At the time with the people that were there, we attempted to merge the detachments, units and battalions which were in existence so as to be able to form a defence staff as well as brigade commands and its units. In the meantime, the corps in Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla and Bihac had been formed. In late November and early December, the 4th Corps was formed in Mostar. That was not in existence previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can return back to IKM [Realtime transcript read in error "EKM"] Zenica that I was discussing earlier, could I please show the witness Exhibit 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, if I could just explain that this is an order from Sefer Halilovic, dated the 28th of April, 1993. So, first of all, General, you see the heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is the Staff of the Supreme Command, the 24th of April, 1993. This is an order for the members of the Staff of the Supreme Command to go out in free territory, indicating the actual names from the people of the Staff and the Minister of Defence, which are to set up a forward command post in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
